title: Kagyu
hookLine: the lineage of Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa

lines: A SHADOW FALLS ACROSS THE PAGE.
THE WORDS, BUT NOT THE MEANING.
cards: A scholar sits reading at a great monastery in India, with books stacked around him. A shadow falls across the page. An old woman, bent and ugly in the story, is standing over him.
She asks whether he understands the words. He says yes, and she laughs with delight. She asks whether he understands the meaning.
He says yes again, and she bursts into tears. You understand the words, she tells him, but not the meaning. The scholar is Naropa.
He puts down his books and goes looking for a teacher. Today: Kagyu.

teach.h: KAGYU: THE LINEAGE OF ORAL INSTRUCTION.
teach.b: First, the name. Kagyu is often rendered the lineage of oral instruction, and some call it the whispered lineage: teaching passed by mouth, from a teacher to a student who is ready, one link at a time.
Second, the Indian links. Tilopa, in the story, was a wild yogi with no monastery at all.

Naropa found him and served him through a long run of hard and strange trials before Tilopa gave him the teaching. Tradition says Tilopa finally struck him on the head with a sandal, and Naropa woke up.

Third, the bridge to Tibet. Marpa was a Tibetan farmer and family man, with a wife and a household, who crossed the mountains to India more than once to study with Naropa, carrying gold to offer and texts to bring home.
He's remembered as Marpa the Translator. Fourth, the student no one would have picked, whom you met in year three.
Milarepa, tradition says, did terrible harm as a young man, using sorcery to take revenge on relatives who had cheated his mother.
Full of remorse, he came to Marpa, who set him to building a stone tower, then ordered him to tear it down, then to build another, and tear that down too. Only after that did Marpa teach him.
Milarepa went into the mountains, lived in caves, and sang his teaching in songs that are still sung. A wild yogi, a scholar, a farmer, a man with a past: no two alike.
The lineage passes anyway, whispered from one to the next.

how: Kagyu Buddhists trace their practice through Tilopa, Naropa, Marpa and Milarepa, receive teachings in person from a teacher, and sing Milarepa's songs.

games.q: you're Naropa. an old woman tells you that you understand the words but not the meaning. what do you do?
o: argue with her and go back to the book.
put down the books and go looking for a teacher.
games.why: Naropa leaves his books and goes looking for Tilopa, the teacher who will give him the meaning.

practice: Say a short line you know by heart, a saying, a verse, a phrase someone gave you, once, slowly.

Then set the words down, the way Naropa set down his books, and stay with what they point to, with no words at all, breath after breath. When the words come back and start repeating, return to the meaning underneath.
